cards.title: Logical SQL Query Execution Order
cards.question: Explain Logical SQL Query Execution Order
cards.answer_30s: SQL is written SELECT-first, but executed logically as: FROM/JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT (and window functions) -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT/OFFSET. This explains why column aliases from SELECT cannot be used in WHERE or GROUP BY.

code.body:
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS emp_count
FROM employees
WHERE active = TRUE
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
ORDER BY emp_count DESC LIMIT 10;

cards.typical_use: Writing bug-free analytical queries and debugging alias/filtering errors.
pitfalls: Remind interviewers: WHERE filters individual rows BEFORE grouping; HAVING filters aggregated groups AFTER GROUP BY.

cards.title: JOIN Types & Anti-Joins
cards.question: Explain JOIN Types & Anti-Joins
cards.answer_30s: INNER JOIN returns matching pairs; LEFT JOIN preserves all left rows (NULLs on non-matching right); FULL OUTER JOIN preserves both; CROSS JOIN produces a Cartesian product. An anti-join (`LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL` or `NOT EXISTS`) finds rows with no match.
cards.typical_use: Finding inactive users, orphaned records, and combining normalized tables.
pitfalls: Always prefer `NOT EXISTS` over `NOT IN` because a single NULL in the subquery causes `NOT IN` to return zero rows.

cards.title: Window Functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG/LEAD)
cards.question: Explain Window Functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG/LEAD)
cards.answer_30s: Window functions compute values across a set of rows related to the current row (`OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)`) without collapsing rows like GROUP BY does. ROW_NUMBER assigns unique sequential ints; RANK leaves gaps on ties; DENSE_RANK has no gaps.

code.body:
SELECT user_id, amount, created_at,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at) AS running_total,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rn
FROM transactions;

cards.typical_use: Top-N per group, running totals, cohort retention, and sessionization.
pitfalls: Top-N per group with a CTE + ROW_NUMBER() is one of the most tested SQL interview patterns.

cards.title: CTEs (Common Table Expressions) vs Subqueries vs Temp Tables
cards.question: Explain CTEs (Common Table Expressions) vs Subqueries vs Temp Tables
cards.answer_30s: CTEs (`WITH ...`) improve readability and support recursion (`WITH RECURSIVE`) for hierarchical trees/graphs. Subqueries inline directly; temporary tables persist for a session and can have their own indexes when intermediate datasets are huge.
cards.typical_use: Traversing org charts, category trees, and multi-step ETL transformations.
pitfalls: Use `WITH RECURSIVE` for hierarchies and multi-step CTEs for clean, modular SQL.

cards.title: Indexing, SARGable Queries & Covering Indexes
cards.question: Explain Indexing, SARGable Queries & Covering Indexes
cards.answer_30s: A query is SARGable (Search ARGument-able) when the planner can use an index. Wrapping an indexed column in a function (e.g. `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at) = 2026` in PostgreSQL or `YEAR(created_at) = 2026` in MySQL) disables the index; rewrite as a range (`created_at >= '2026-01-01'`). Covering indexes (`INCLUDE` in PostgreSQL) satisfy queries directly from the index without heap lookups.
cards.typical_use: Eliminating full table scans and achieving fast Index-Only Scans.
pitfalls: Avoid leading wildcards `LIKE '%term'` on B-Tree indexes—use full-text search or trigram GIN indexes instead.

cards.title: Normalization (1NF-3NF) vs Denormalization
cards.question: Explain Normalization (1NF-3NF) vs Denormalization
cards.answer_30s: Normalization removes redundancy and update anomalies: 1NF (atomic values), 2NF (no partial dependency on composite key), 3NF (no transitive dependencies). Denormalization intentionally duplicates data (e.g. storing order_total or star-schema fact/dimension tables) to eliminate expensive joins in OLAP/read-heavy systems.

code.body: -- OLTP: normalized foreign keys | OLAP: star schema fact + dimensions

cards.typical_use: Designing OLTP transactional schemas vs analytical data warehouses.
pitfalls: Normalize by default for OLTP correctness; denormalize selectively based on measured read bottlenecks.

cards.title: ACID Transactions & Isolation Anomalies
cards.question: Explain ACID Transactions & Isolation Anomalies
cards.answer_30s: SQL defines 4 isolation levels against 3 classic anomalies: Dirty Reads (reading uncommitted data), Non-Repeatable Reads (same row changes between reads), and Phantom Reads (new matching rows appear). Read Committed prevents dirty reads; Repeatable Read prevents non-repeatable reads; Serializable prevents all three.
pitfalls: Atomic conditional UPDATE (`WHERE qty >= 1`) often beats read-then-write locking.

cards.title: Q: Write a SQL query to find the 2nd highest salary (or Top-N per department).
cards.question: Q: Write a SQL query to find the 2nd highest salary (or Top-N per department).
cards.answer_30s: A: Use DENSE_RANK() inside a CTE so ties are handled cleanly without skipping ranks, and return NULL/empty cleanly if fewer than 2 distinct salaries exist.
pitfalls: Always clarify with the interviewer how ties should be handled (RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER).

cards.title: Q: How do you find and remove duplicate rows in SQL?
cards.question: Q: How do you find and remove duplicate rows in SQL?
cards.answer_30s: A: Use ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by the natural key columns and delete where rn > 1, or group by the key with HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 to inspect duplicates first.
cards.typical_use: Data cleaning and adding unique constraints to legacy tables.
pitfalls: After deduplicating, add a UNIQUE constraint/index so duplicates cannot re-enter.

cards.title: Q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)?
cards.question: Q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)?
cards.answer_30s: A: WHERE filters rows before grouping (cannot reference aggregates); HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY. COUNT(*) counts all rows including NULLs, whereas COUNT(col) counts only non-NULL values in that column (and COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique non-NULL values).

code.body:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS total, COUNT(shipped_at) AS shipped
FROM orders GROUP BY status HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;

cards.typical_use: Avoiding subtle off-by-NULL bugs in reporting queries.
pitfalls: Remind interviewers that `SUM` and `AVG` also ignore NULLs—`COALESCE(col, 0)` changes AVG denominator!

cards.title: Q: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP?
cards.question: Q: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP?
cards.answer_30s: A: DELETE removes specific rows via WHERE, logs every row deletion, fires triggers, and can be rolled back. TRUNCATE deallocates all table pages/data in O(1) without scanning rows (resetting identity sequences if requested). DROP removes both data and table schema/indexes completely.

code.body:
-- PostgreSQL: resets sequences atomically
TRUNCATE TABLE temp_staging RESTART IDENTITY;

cards.typical_use: Clearing large staging tables safely without bloating transaction logs.
pitfalls: Note that in PostgreSQL, even TRUNCATE and DROP are transactional and can be rolled back inside a BEGIN/ROLLBACK block.

cards.title: Q: How does SQL handle NULL in comparisons and joins?
cards.question: Q: How does SQL handle NULL in comparisons and joins?
cards.answer_30s: A: NULL represents unknown, not zero or empty string. Any arithmetic or comparison with NULL (`col = NULL`, `col != NULL`) evaluates to UNKNOWN, which WHERE treats as false. Always use `IS NULL`, `IS NOT NULL`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, or `COALESCE()`.
cards.typical_use: Preventing silent data loss in filters and anti-joins.
pitfalls: In GROUP BY and UNIQUE constraints, NULLs are grouped together (and in SQL standard, distinct NULLs don't violate UNIQUE unless NULLS NOT DISTINCT is set).

cards.title: Q: How do you optimize a slow SQL query step by step?
cards.question: Q: How do you optimize a slow SQL query step by step?
cards.answer_30s: A: 1) Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to locate full table scans, high-cost nested loops, or bad row estimates. 2) Add missing composite/covering indexes matching WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY. 3) Make predicates SARGable and avoid SELECT *. 4) Replace deep OFFSET with keyset pagination. 5) Pre-aggregate or partition massive tables.

code.body:
-- PostgreSQL syntax
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT id FROM events WHERE user_id = 12 AND created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days';

pitfalls: Always mention checking index selectivity and avoiding unnecessary `DISTINCT` or `ORDER BY` on huge intermediate sets.

cards.title: Q: What is the N+1 query problem and how do you solve it in SQL/ORMs?
cards.question: Q: What is the N+1 query problem and how do you solve it in SQL/ORMs?
cards.answer_30s: A: N+1 happens when code runs 1 query to fetch N parent records and then executes N separate queries in a loop to fetch each parent's children. Fix by using a single JOIN, `WHERE parent_id IN (...)`, or ORM eager loading (`select_related` / `joinedload` / DataLoader).
cards.typical_use: Eliminating 100x latency amplification in API endpoints.
pitfalls: Mention that ORMs hide N+1 queries behind lazy attribute access—enable SQL query logging in dev/tests to catch them.
